# High Income Child Benefit Charge, in plain English

Figures: 2026-27. The rules this text is printed from are proved equal to the model's own definitions for every input and every parameter set (`hicbcRule_eval`); see [README.md](README.md) for what that does and does not cover.

## High Income Child Benefit Charge (ITEPA 2003 s681C)

To work out the High Income Child Benefit Charge:

1. Start with the Child Benefit paid for the tax year.
2. If that is not a whole number of pounds, round it down to the whole pound (drop the pence).
3. Take a percentage of that: 1% for every whole £200 by which your adjusted net income is more than £60,000, up to 100%. Only whole steps of £200 count, so the percentage is a whole number.
4. If that is not a whole number of pounds, round it down to the whole pound (drop the pence).

**Child Benefit for the year** means the Child Benefit paid for the tax year (6 April to 5 April) to you, or to a partner you live with if you have the higher adjusted net income of the two. Only the partner with the higher income pays the charge.

**Adjusted net income** means your total income for the year that income tax is charged on, before any allowances, less the gross amount of any Gift Aid donations and of any pension contributions paid to a scheme that claims the tax relief for you.

For example, with £2,337.40 of Child Benefit (two children for 52 weeks):

| Adjusted net income | The High Income Child Benefit Charge |
| --- | --- |
| £60,000 | £0 |
| £60,199.99 | £0 |
| £60,200 | £23 |
| £70,000 | £1,168 |
| £79,999.99 | £2,313 |
| £80,000 | £2,337 |
| £90,000 | £2,337 |

At 100% the charge equals the Child Benefit rounded down to the pound, so above that income none of the Child Benefit is kept.
